newsitem.title: USA: New U.S. corporate bond deals seen well bid.
newsitem.headline: New U.S. corporate bond deals seen well bid.

text.p: Strong investor demand for new U.S. corporate bonds is prompting companies to increase the size of their existing deals and is luring more issuers to the market this week, syndicate officials said.
Norfolk Southern Corp's $3.65 billion seven-tranche debt offering, which is expected to price on Wednesday, may be increased to as much as $4.3 billion, market players said.

"This is a rare opportunity to buy railroad bonds," said one trader. "This company is also rated higher than CSX (which recently sold $2.5 billion in debt), and looking out a year, the company may be a single-A credit."
Norfolk Southern's offering is rated BAA1/BBB-plus. CSX's recent deal was rated BAA2/BBB.
While Norfolk Southern's offering is expected to dominate the market's attention on Wednesday, other issuers are already preparing high-grade deals for later in the week.
CIGNA Inc plans to sell $600 million in 10-year and 30-year bonds via Goldman Sachs & Co as early as Thursday, a company official confirmed. The bonds are rated A3/A-minus.
Proceeds from the offering will be used to finance the insurance company's purchase of Healthsource Inc, an HMO company for $1.65 billion, the official said.
In the high-yield bond market, Sun Media Corp plans to sell $90 million in 10-year senior subordinated notes in a 144a private placement on Wednesday.
Price talk on the deal, which is rated B3/B-minus, is in the 9 5/8 percent area, market sources said. CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Inc will underwrite the offering.
Proceeds from the offering will be used to finance the company's purchase of the London Free Press and Netmar Inc, a shopper and weekly paper publisher in Canada, sources said.

With the completion of the acquisitions, Sun Media said the company will become the second largest daily newspaper publishing group in Canada, based on circulation. The company also owns The Toronto Sun and The Financial Post.
Sun Media sold $150 million in 9.50 percent senior subordinated notes due '07 in February in order to refinance bank debt acquired in connection with a management-led buyout of the company in 1996.
Early on Wednesday, Radio One Inc, a U.S. radio broadcaster specializing in African-American programming, sold $75 million in senior subordinated notes due '04.
The company had postponed the deal, which was originally scheduled to price in April, due to poor market conditions.

The securities, which are not rated, were priced to yield 12 percent but have a "split-coupon" structure. The notes were sold at a discount of 87.742 and pay a seven percent coupon for the first three-years. Subsequently, their coupon steps up to 12 percent.
Credit Suisse First Boston and NationsBanc Capital Markets acted as joint lead managers for the 144a offering.

Other 144a high-yield offerings expected to price later this week include a $470 million four-year zero coupon deal from a holding company of Coleman Co Inc, and a $400 million 10-year senior note deal from Williams Scotsman Inc, market sources said.
